hook: A school report shows two bars for the percent of students passing a state exam: one school at 52%, the other at 58%. The second bar looks four times as tall. Is the second school four times better? No: the vertical axis starts at 50%. Graphs of categorical data are simple, but they have rules, and those rules are what keep a picture honest.

prereq.q: In a sample of 200, the relative frequency of a category is 0.15. What is its count?
When do the relative frequencies of a categorical variable add to 1?
options: When each individual is in exactly one category
Only when there are two categories
prereq.why: Then the categories together make up the whole sample.

figure.caption: The same relative frequencies as a bar chart and as a pie chart. Bars are easier to compare; the pie shows parts of one whole.

chain.cause: Each category of a categorical variable gets one bar
chain.effect: the bar’s height is the category’s count or relative frequency, measured from 0
bars can go in any order and are drawn with gaps between them

chain.cause: When each individual is in exactly one category
chain.effect: the parts make one whole, so a pie chart can show them as slices

chain.cause: A cut-off axis or bars from groups of different sizes
chain.effect: the picture misleads, so start at 0 and graph relative frequencies to compare groups

ideas: A bar chart shows one bar per category, with height equal to the count or relative frequency. The vertical axis starts at 0.
A pie chart shows each category as a slice of one circle, sized by its relative frequency. It needs categories that do not overlap and cover everyone.
Bar charts make it easier to compare categories; pie charts show how parts make up a whole.
To compare groups of different sizes, graph relative frequencies, and describe what the graph shows with numbers, in context.

misconception.wrong: School B’s bar is four times as tall, so its pass rate is four times school A’s.
misconception.right: The axis starts at 50%. The actual rates are 58% and 52%, a difference of 6 percentage points.

summary: Bar charts and pie charts display one categorical variable. A bar’s height is its count or relative frequency measured from 0; a pie’s slices are parts of one whole, so every individual must be in exactly one category. Compare groups of different sizes with relative frequencies, and check axes before trusting a picture.
